subject: Business
title: Make vs. Buy Decisions
description: A fast breakdown of Make vs. Buy Decisions for builders.

hook.text: Should Nike make its own shoes or hire factories in Vietnam? The answer shaped a $50 billion company.

buildup.text: The make-or-buy decision: produce in-house for control, or outsource for cost savings and flexibility.

discovery.text: Core competencies should stay in-house. Non-core activities can often be outsourced more efficiently.

twist.text: Outsourcing too much can leave you dependent on others for critical capabilities.

climax.text: The best companies outsource commodity work and invest in what makes them unique.

punchline.text: Make what makes you special. Buy everything else.

quiz.question: What should companies generally keep in-house?
options: Core competencies that make them unique

details.summary: Make-versus-buy decisions determine whether a company produces components internally or purchases them from outside suppliers. The analysis weighs factors including cost, quality control, core competency focus, capacity, intellectual property protection, and supply security.
details.whyItMatters: Make-versus-buy choices shape a company's competitive position and cost structure for years. Outsourcing non-core activities frees resources for innovation, but over-outsourcing can erode capabilities and create dangerous supplier dependencies.
takeaways: Total cost analysis must include hidden costs of both making and buying
Core competencies should generally be kept in-house to protect advantage
Transaction cost economics guides the boundary between firm and market

faq.question: What factors favor making a component in-house?
faq.answer: Core competency requiring proprietary knowledge, need for tight quality control, protection of intellectual property, sufficient production volume to achieve economies of scale, and strategic importance of maintaining internal capabilities all favor in-house production.

faq.question: What hidden costs should be included in a make-versus-buy analysis?
faq.answer: For making: equipment depreciation, facility overhead, management attention, quality systems, and opportunity cost of capital. For buying: supplier qualification, quality inspection, logistics, contract management, and risk of supply disruption or quality failures.
